newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - HK handover evokes memories for Chelsea pensioner.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK handover evokes memories for Chelsea pensioner.

text.p: When Reg Truss was serving in Hong Kong with the British army in the 1950s, his main difficulty with his Chinese landlord was to persuade him to cook roast beef rather than curried rice.

Now, as the colony reverts to Peking, Truss has dusted down his collection of photograph albums which include faded pictures of his old barracks where Chinese troops are now beginning to take up residence.

At the age of 80, Truss is a Chelsea Pensioner, a member of a small group of veterans who live at London's Royal Hospital and are a familiar sight around the capital in their distinctive red coats and dark caps.
In 1950, after an eventful World War Two career that included being evacuated from Dunkirk in 1940, he sailed for Hong Kong with his artillery unit.
Along with the rest of his kit he had packed the cameras that were to occupy much of his spare time.

As Hong Kong's new leader Tung Chee-hwa hoisted China's red flag over Government House, seat of the departing colonial governor, Truss turned to the pictures he took in 1953, when Queen Elizabeth was crowned.
The colony and its British army garrison celebrated the London coronation with enthusiasm, staging parades and parties.
"They made a great fuss of it," he said.
Truss's album shows there was hardly a public building which did not have "God Save the Queen" or "Long Live the Queen" emblazoned in large elaborate signs.
"They were held up with bamboo," Truss recalled. "Very clever, the Chinese."
Teams of Chinese men staged dragon parades and walked on stilts along the colony's streets while British military policemen in peaked caps, shorts and knee-length socks kept order.
His photos make clear, however, that official China did not share the colony's enthusiasm for things British, even in those days.
While the Hong Kong and Shanghai Bank building is decorated with a large crown to mark the coronation, a neighbouring Chinese bank building is bare.
Truss recalls that Mao Zedong's newly proclaimed People's Republic of China just across the frontier played havoc with the dark room he set up in his bathroom to develop and print his pictures.

"Mao stopped at the border, but he controlled the water supply," Truss said. "He turned it off and my photography suffered a lot. It was his way of saying 'you've got the island but you haven't got the water'."
He added: "We were watching every move he was making."
Truss was part of a locating unit, 15 Observation Battery, charged with identifying where Chinese forces were and relaying that information to British gunners.
But for the most part his photograph albums provide an essentially peaceful portrait of colonial and service life in Hong Kong after World War Two.
His pictures show him and his wife May and daughter Linda at the seaside, at parties and at outings to the Tiger Balm Garden, established by the inventor of the famous cure-all.
Truss's gunner friends are shown in khaki shorts while on duty, in white uniform coats at mess dinners and in drag for a "comic football match".
A man in a swimming costume sits on the beach, drinking tea from a china cup and saucer.
"We lived a normal family life, with guests and friends from the navy as well as the army. We had our own Chinese servants who cooked for us and did housework," he recalled.

When he and his family first arrived, they lived in a hotel because the colony had no other means of housing the growing British garrison that moved in after the end of Japan's wartime military occupation.
"Our hotel was run by a Chinese manager. His main difficult job was to produce roast beef instead of curried rice," Truss said.
"There were about 30 people staying so he did very well out of us. My wife became an expert at Mahjong."
In 1954 it was time for Truss and his family to return home from Hong Kong. They left the colony in the same way the British army always leaves -- to the sound of a military band.
In his retirement, Truss lives with his pictures and his memories at the Royal Hospital, founded by King Charles II for old and disabled soldiers in 1682, although he is spry enough.
"I don't suppose there's another collection of photographs like mine in the country," he said.
